introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry twenty-five marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

La règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées sans source consultable. Les exemples cites sont des exemples reconnus ; aucune statistique precise n'est avancee. Les faits cites sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.
Points : (6 + 6) + (6 + 7) = 25, conformes au sujet. Les sous-parties (i) et (ii) du sujet restent dans le texte des sous-questions a et b ; leurs points sont additionnés (a = 12, b = 13).

Faits cités avec prudence : le glissement de terrain de Gouache (Bafoussam) en octobre 2019 est cité comme ayant fait de nombreuses victimes, sans chiffre ; le Mont Cameroun est dit avoir erupté plusieurs fois ces dernières décennies, sans date. À faire vérifier.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) You have observed sudden downslope movement of soil and weathered rock materials in your community with considerable material damage and loss in human lives.

(i) Briefly explain THREE causes of such movements. (6 marks)

(ii) Propose THREE measures that can be used to reduce the impacts of such movements. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sudden downslope movement of soil and weathered rock (a **landslide**, rock slide, mudflow or slump) is a form of **mass movement**. In Cameroon the steep, deeply weathered slopes of the western highlands and of the hillsides of towns such as Bafoussam, Bamenda and Yaounde are prone to it in the rainy season; the landslide at Gouache, Bafoussam, in October 2019 caused many deaths.

**(i) Three causes.**

1. **Heavy or prolonged rainfall.** Water fills the pores of the regolith, which makes the material heavier, reduces the friction and cohesion between the particles (the pore water pressure pushes the grains apart) and lubricates the slip surface, so that the slope fails. Most mass movements in Cameroon occur at the peak of the rainy season.
2. **Steep slopes and undercutting or loading of the slope by people.** Cutting into the base of the slope for roads, houses and quarries removes support, and building on the upper part adds weight. The slope becomes steeper than its angle of stability. Natural undercutting by a river or the sea has the same effect.
3. **Removal of vegetation.** Deforestation and clearing for farming and housing remove the roots that bind the soil together and the leaves that intercept the rain, and they reduce the removal of water by transpiration, so that the soil is wetter and weaker. Weak, deeply weathered rock or clay and earth tremors or vibrations (earthquakes, blasting, heavy traffic) are other causes.

**(ii) Three measures to reduce the impacts.**

1. **Afforestation and planting of vegetation cover** (deep-rooted trees, grasses, bamboo) on the slopes, with the protection of the remaining forest, to bind the soil and take up water.
2. **Engineering structures and drainage:** retaining walls and gabions at the foot of the slope, terracing, slope reduction, and surface and underground drains that carry the water away from the slope, so that the soil does not become saturated.
3. **Land-use planning and early warning:** forbid or control building on steep and unstable slopes and in the paths of landslides (hazard maps and zoning), resettle the families living in the danger zones, monitor the slopes and the rainfall, give early warning and train and educate the community (evacuation plans). Strict control of road cuts and quarrying is also needed.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Irrespective of the challenges, why do people still live in volcanic regions? (6 marks)

(ii) Examine TWO strategies that people living in volcanic regions may adopt to offset the negative effects of volcanic hazards. (7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Why people live in volcanic regions in spite of the hazards.**

1. **Fertile soils.** Weathered lava and volcanic ash are rich in minerals (potassium, phosphorus, magnesium and others) and give deep fertile soils, which support intensive farming and dense populations (around Mount Cameroon, with its tea, banana, rubber and oil palm plantations; the slopes of Mount Etna and Vesuvius in Italy; Java in Indonesia).
2. **Economic resources and employment.** Volcanic areas provide **geothermal energy** (Iceland), minerals such as sulphur, building stone, pumice and thermal springs, and the **tourism** attracted by the scenery, climbing and hot springs creates jobs and income.
3. **Cooler and healthier climate of the highlands, scenery and water.** Volcanic highlands, such as the Bamenda highlands, are cooler and better watered than the lowlands.
4. **Low frequency of eruptions and lack of choice.** Eruptions are rare compared with the length of a lifetime, so the risk seems small to people; many cannot afford to move or have no other land, and they have strong family, cultural and religious attachments to the area where their ancestors lived. Governments also promote the use of the resources of these areas.

**(ii) Two strategies to offset the negative effects of volcanic hazards.**

1. **Monitoring, prediction, early warning and evacuation.** Volcano observatories monitor the volcano with seismometers (earthquake swarms), tilt meters and GPS (swelling of the cone), gas and temperature measurements and satellite images, so that a forecast can be made. Warning systems, evacuation routes and shelters, and regular drills and education of the population allow people to leave before the eruption, which saves lives (the volcano observatories of Japan and Italy, the evacuation plans around Mount Merapi in Indonesia or Vesuvius). The population has to be informed and trained for these measures to be effective.
2. **Land-use planning and protective engineering.** Hazard maps show the zones at risk from lava flows, ash fall, lahars (mudflows) and gases, and building in the most dangerous zones is restricted. Buildings are designed to carry ash loads (steep roofs, strong frames); lava flows can be diverted or cooled with barriers, channels and sea water (as attempted in Iceland and on Etna); and dams and channels may control lahars. Other adjustments are to diversify income, to insure property and to store food and water, so that the community recovers faster after an eruption.

Mount Cameroon has eruptéd several times in recent decades, so these strategies are relevant to the Buea region.
